content: Calcium sulfate is a widely used chemical in both laboratory and industrial settings. In its γ-anhydrite form, which is nearly anhydrous, it serves as a desiccant to absorb moisture. It is also employed as a coagulant in food products like tofu. In its natural state, unrefined calcium sulfate appears as a translucent, crystalline white rock. When marketed under the trade name Drierite, it is often blue or pink due to the addition of cobalt chloride, which acts as a moisture indicator. The dihydrate form of calcium sulfate (CaSO₄·2H₂O) naturally occurs as gypsum, while the anhydrous form is found as β-anhydrite. Depending on the calcination process applied to calcium sulfate dihydrate, two specific hemihydrate forms can be produced: alpha-hemihydrate and beta-hemihydrate. These forms differ primarily in their crystal size. The primary sources of calcium sulfate are naturally occurring gypsum and anhydrite, which are found globally as evaporite deposits. These materials can be extracted through open-cast quarrying or deep mining. The global production of natural gypsum is approximately 100 million tonnes annually. Additionally, calcium sulfate can be obtained as a byproduct of industrial processes. For example, flue gases from power plants and cement manufacturing are treated with finely ground limestone or lime to reduce sulfur oxide emissions, producing an impure calcium sulfite that oxidizes to calcium sulfate upon storage. Similarly, in the production of phosphoric acid from phosphate rock, calcium phosphate is treated with sulfuric acid, precipitating calcium sulfate. In hydrogen fluoride production, calcium fluoride is treated with sulfuric acid, also yielding calcium sulfate. During zinc refining, zinc sulfate solutions are treated with lime to co-precipitate heavy metals like barium, forming calcium sulfate. Calcium sulfate can also be recovered and reused from scrap drywall at construction sites. However, these precipitation processes often concentrate radioactive elements in the calcium sulfate product, particularly in phosphate byproducts, as phosphate rocks naturally contain actinides. The phosphate industry alone generates over 200 million tonnes of calcium sulfate waste annually. When gypsum is heated to temperatures between 100°C and 150°C, it undergoes partial dehydration, losing approximately 75% of its chemically bound water. The exact temperature and duration required depend on the ambient partial pressure of water vapor. Industrial calcination processes may use temperatures as high as 170°C, at which point γ-anhydrite begins to form. Dehydration, also known as calcination, starts at around 80°C, although some dehydration can occur as low as 50°C in dry air. The heat energy applied during this process is primarily used to drive off water as vapor, rather than significantly increasing the mineral's temperature. Once the water is removed, the temperature of the material rises more rapidly. This endothermic reaction is exploited in drywall to provide fire resistance. During a fire, the gypsum in drywall loses water, keeping the structure behind it relatively cool and delaying damage to wooden or steel framing, thereby preventing or significantly slowing structural collapse. Unlike most minerals, which form liquid or semi-liquid pastes when rehydrated, calcined gypsum exhibits a unique property. When mixed with water at ambient temperatures, it rapidly reverts chemically to its dihydrate form while physically setting into a rigid and strong crystal lattice. This exothermic reaction allows gypsum to be easily cast into various shapes, such as sheets for drywall, sticks for blackboard chalk, and molds for immobilizing broken bones or for metal casting. When combined with polymers, it has been used as a bone repair cement. Small amounts of calcined gypsum can also be added to soil to create strong structures directly from cast earth, offering an alternative to adobe, which loses strength when wet. The conditions of dehydration can be adjusted to modify the porosity of the hemihydrate, resulting in the so-called alpha and beta hemihydrates, which are chemically nearly identical. γ-Anhydrite reacts slowly with water to revert to the dihydrate state, a property utilized in some commercial desiccants. When heated above 250°C, the completely anhydrous form, known as β-anhydrite or natural anhydrite, is formed. Natural anhydrite does not react with water, even over geological timescales, unless it is finely ground. The variable composition of the hemihydrate and γ-anhydrite, as well as their easy interconversion, is due to their nearly identical crystal structures, which contain channels capable of accommodating varying amounts of water or other small molecules like methanol.
